newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan media questions 'scapegoating' of Peru envoy.
newsitem.headline: Japan media questions 'scapegoating' of Peru envoy.

text.p: Major Japanese newspapers said on Wednesday that the sacking of Japan's ambassador to Peru was premature and he had been made a scapegoat for the Lima hostage crisis.

Veteran diplomat Morihisa Aoki, 58, whose grace under fire during the four-month crisis was widely admired outside of Japan, had been forced in a symbolic way to commit hara-kiri, samurai-style suicide by disembowelment, one daily newspaper said.

"He was forced to perform 'hara-kiri'. Instead of a government decision it was left to public opinion to turn his dismissal into a drama, which leaves a bad aftertaste," the liberal Asahi Shimbun said in an editorial.

Aoki's resignation was accepted on Tuesday after he offered to step down to take responsibility for security lapses that allowed 14 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels to storm a reception at his residence in Lima last December 17 and take hundreds of guests hostage.

Most of them, except for Aoki and 71 fellow hostages, were released in the weeks before the siege ended on April 22, when a daring operation by Peruvian commandos took the rebels by surprise during their daily game of indoor soccer.
The Yomiuri Shimbun, a conservative daily often sympathetic to government policy, said the surprise announcement in parliament had put in doubt an inquiry into the affair.

"It smacks of an overly hasty dismissal. This calls into question both the Foreign Ministry's inquiry into the incident, due to be completed by the end of June, and the possibility of a serious approach by the government towards preventing a recurrence," the daily said.

The business daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun said Aoki-bashers were provoked by the image of a pale and drawn Aoki chain smoking his way through a news conference shortly after his rescue and displaying what some considered a brash demeanor.

"He is a very straightforward person and his kind of proud behaviour and tone is hard to accept in a society which glorifies humility," the financial daily said. "However, making the ambassador a scapegoat is not the end of the matter by far. There remains the question: Is it possible to completely rule out terrorist acts, whatever countermeasures you take?" the paper added.
"But most Japanese are not ready for the 'resolute stance against terrorism' advocated by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto," the Nihon Keizai said.
Ordinary Japanese were disgruntled with earlier media criticism of Aoki and held mixed views of the government's handling of his dismissal.

"It's not fair of the media to blow up parts of Aoki's comments and then clamour for him to take responsibility," said Mari Saito, 47, a former flight attendant who was on a plane hijacked by Palestinian guerrillas in December 1973.
"I feel sorry for Mr Aoki," she said.
An 80-year old retired businessman said: "I cannot understand why the government is doing this. And hasn't Peru asked that Mr Aoki be sent back as ambassador again?"
Fifty-one-year-old businessman Yukio Tomita, however, believed the decision was just.
"I think the government did the right thing in firing him. He must bear the responsibility for security," Tomita said.
